    COMMENTS OF NRG ENERGY, INC. IN RESPONSE TO PROPOSED RULE ON
                   TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY
         NRG Energy, Inc. (NRG) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the proposal
to revise and adopt rules (Proposed Rule) 1 related to the directive in Senate Bill 6 (SB6) 2 for the
Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) to modify the methodology for transmission
cost recovery and allocation and evolve away from the existing four coincident peak (4CP)
methodology. NRG is the parent company of retail electric providers (REPs) and power generation
companies (PGCs) with longstanding experience in the competitive electricity markets in Texas.

                                             I.        INTRODUCTION

         The growth of large loads and data centers presents significant opportunity for Texas and
is necessary to secure our place as a leader in artificial intelligence, national security, and the digital
future. But that growth must be managed in a way that preserves the availability, reliability, and
affordability of electricity to all consumers. To reduce the impact on consumers, NRG is a strong
supporter of “grid-friendly” bring your own generation (BYOG) and flexible load arrangements
and for reforming how transmission costs are funded, as contemplated by SB6. The infrastructure
required to support the coming growth is significant, and large loads should pay for their fair share
of it.

         To that end, the Commission’s proposed reform of the current 4CP transmission cost
allocation methodology is necessary and should reduce the potential for cost shifting to residential
customers, which should be one of the primary objectives. NRG supports the Proposed Rule’s

However, the calculation of the minimum billing demand should be designed to differentiate
between large load customers that bring new generation, co-locate with generation, or agree to

on how to revise the Proposed Rule to appropriately account for the benefits of those arrangements.

                          II.      RESPONSE TO PREAMBLE QUESTIONS

         NRG responds below to the questions posed in the preamble to the Proposed Rule:

Q1.      Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
         be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
         different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

         NRG Response: Yes. While NRG supports the incorporation of a minimum billing demand
feature to minimize cost shifting from large loads to residential consumers along with the proposed
move from 4CP to 12CP, the minimum billing demand should reflect the large load customer’s
utilization of the transmission system and how transmission costs are incurred. If a large load
customer will interconnect in a way that will not use the ERCOT system as much as other large
load customers, especially during peak demand periods, the minimum billing demand should
reflect this difference. Specifically, the methodology should appropriately account for
arrangements that are designed to minimize the use of the transmission system, such as the
customer’s registration with ERCOT as a Withdrawal-Limited Private Use Network (WLPUN) or
Provisional Controllable Load Resource (PCLR), 4 or the customer’s proposed co-location with

up in summer, which may not result in a meaningful change to the allocation compared to today.
          4

at least one Large Load, with an established MW Withdrawal limit at a single Point of Interconnection (POI)

and PCLR registration are paths that allow for potential inclusion in Batch Zero, conditioned, respectively, on the
WLPUN’s and PCLR’s willingness to accept limitations on how much power they can consume from the grid until
the transmission system can accommodate their full demand. See generally Nodal Protocol Revision Request (NPRR)
1325, PUCT Report (Jun. 18, 2026); Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) 145, PUCT Report (Jun. 18, 2026);
see also PGRR 145, ERCOT Comments (May 2, 2026) & ERCOT Comments (Apr. 17, 2026).

new generation (i.e., BYOG) 5 or with existing generation in a net metering arrangement (NMA).
These arrangements—i.e., WLPUN, PCLR, BYOG, and NMA—benefit the grid by minimizing
the use of the transmission system, especially during times when the transmission system is
congested, and therefore should receive credit in the determination of their minimum billing
demand.

         In BYOG/WLPUN arrangements particularly, large load customers are helping to fund the
construction of new generation to improve resource adequacy and relieve stress on the
transmission system. Therefore, these arrangements should be encouraged to the greatest extent
possible. Governor Abbott has recognized the need to support and prioritize BYOG arrangements
and has made it a priority in his direction to the PUCT and ERCOT as well as recent public
statements. 6,7,8 The rule should not impose a minimum billing demand and resulting charge that
ignores the contribution of the new co-located generation, because such a charge would
disincentivize the very BYOG arrangements that the Governor seeks to incentivize—i.e., by
charging the large load for a presumed maximum usage of the transmission grid over a 20 year
period even though that large load would be served by its own generation and would not fully use
the transmission system (especially during peak periods). Therefore, the minimum billing demand
for BYOG arrangements, in particular, should recognize the expected capacity contribution from
the co-located generation during system peak demand. A similar credit is appropriate for other
grid-friendly arrangements like PCLR and NMA. NRG proposes a methodology to do so in
response to Question 2.

Q2.     Should the large load minimum billing demand be:
        a.       fixed for 20 years as proposed;
        b.       reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or
        c.       extended to a longer time period?

        NRG Response: As stated above, NRG supports the incorporation of the minimum billing
demand as a means to allocate transmission costs to large loads to mitigate cost shifting to other
consumer classes, particularly the residential class. In prior comments, 14 NRG proposed an
alternative methodology for transmission cost allocation that would utilize a cost ceiling for non-
large load customers and increase the share of future transmission costs allocated to large loads
since large load growth (and particularly, large computational load) is the primary driver for current
and future transmission system development. A minimum billing demand component for large
loads can accomplish a similar objective as NRG’s proposed cost ceiling, but it should be designed
to not be overly punitive to large loads in general or discourage “grid friendly” arrangements such
as BYOG arrangements, by employing a phased reduction as detailed further below.

        More precisely, while the proposed minimum billing demand rightfully helps ensure that
large loads contribute to system upgrade costs, if Texas is to continue to be viewed as “open for
business,” the cost allocation methodology should begin to recognize actual transmission system
utilization by large loads during peak periods sooner than 20 years and should immediately credit
(and thereby incentivize) large load arrangements that contribute to grid reliability. The 12CP
approach in the Proposed Rule does a much better job of reflecting system utilization than 4CP
and will better capture the system utilization of large loads that are designed to be flexible like
BYOG/WLPUN, PCLR, and NMA arrangements. However, that will be true only if 12CP is
coupled with a phased (rather than static) minimum billing demand concept; otherwise, the
minimum billing demand will always be the “greater of” number compared to 12CP and will thus
set the billing demand (making actual 12CP usage irrelevant) for 20 years. In addition, the proposal
to use the higher of the contracted demand or non-coincident peak (NCP) demand for calculating


implemented and agreed to by ERCOT.”) (emphasis added); see also ERCOT Planning Guide §§ 9.3.2.2, 9.5.4
(explaining that for WLPUNs, the withdrawal limit is based on a determination of how much load the grid can reliably
serve when the co-located generation is off).

should not ever use more than its “contracted demand” as the Proposed Rule would define that

NRG recommends removing NCP from the methodology.

         To strike a balance between ensuring that large loads appropriately contribute to system
upgrade costs without discouraging their investment in Texas, and to appropriately recognize the
value of, and incentivize, co-location and other grid friendly arrangements, NRG recommends a
phased reduction of the minimum billing demand across the proposed 20-year period for both
stand-alone large loads and co-located large loads, 15 with a different starting point and reduction
schedule for each scenario. NRG’s specific proposal, below, is illustrative, but whatever the
Commission adopts should, at a minimum, differentiate co-located arrangements from stand-alone
arrangements when establishing the minimum billing demand and should include a phased
reduction over time for all large loads.

         Specifically, NRG proposes the following phased schedule. First, for large loads that are
not co-located with generation (or registered with ERCOT as a PCLR), the minimum billing
demand should be 100% of contracted demand in the first 5 years, 75% in the second 5-year period,
50% in the third 5-year period, and 25% in the fourth 5-year period. Second, for BYOG or other
grid friendly arrangements, NRG recommends a phased reduction starting with the minimum
billing demand at 50% of contracted demand in the first 5 years, 25% in the second 5-year period,
15% in the third 5-year period, and 10% in the fourth 5-year period, with the additional caveat that
a WLPUN or PCLR should have its minimum demand capped by the applicable withdrawal limit
(e.g., if that limit is lower than 50% of contracted demand in the first 5 years, the minimum demand

Q3:    Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand
       lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large
       load minimum billing demand:
       a.      reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand
               is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum
               NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline
               in phases over the years, and how?

       NRG Response: In the response to Question 2, NRG recommended a phased reduction of
the use of the minimum billing demand for large loads as part of the 12CP allocation. In addition
to a phased reduction, the Commission should incorporate an adjustment to the minimum billing
demand for large loads that are part of a co-location arrangement with generation such as a
BYOG/WLPUN or an NMA or are registered as a PCLR. Large loads that are part of those
arrangements will naturally not utilize the transmission system as much and likely will not require
the same amount of system upgrades. There should be recognition of this lower cost contribution
in the allocation methodology. If co-location will be with an intermittent resource, as an alternative
to the suggested phasing percentages in Question 2, the Commission could make an adjustment to
the contracted peak demand for the large load customer based on the Effective Load Carrying
Capability (ELCC) of the co-located generation resource.

       b.      be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
               load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
               customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
               year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
               weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
               over the years, and how?

       NRG Response: NRG recommends the adjustment to the minimum billing demand for
large load arrangements co-located with generation as stated in the response to Questions 2 and
3a. Other than during construction delays, a large load customer’s contracted peak demand and
highest NCP demand during the year should be identical. Based on the Proposed Rule’s

Q5.    Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include
       transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to
       serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

       NRG Response: NRG does not recommend this approach. Transmission projects
recommended as part of the batch study are likely required to provide system upgrades and serve
multiple customers or even regions of the ERCOT system. These upgrades will be used on an
ongoing basis to serve the broader system needs. This type of cost seems more appropriate to
allocate through the minimum demand charge and 12CP methodology. Interconnection costs are
typically specific to the direct interconnection facilities for an individual customer (i.e., the
driveway). Upgrades to the transmission system beyond interconnection facilities are typically
utilized and shared among many customers.

Q6.    If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
       whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,
       how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments
       and transmission planning studies?

       NRG Response: The load forecast used for resource adequacy reports and transmission
planning should utilize the load commissioning plan (LCP) (adjusted to account for any applicable
MW withdrawal limit) that is part of a large load interconnection request that has an executed and
securitized interconnection agreement, unless the agreement is terminated due to unutilized
capacity. Construction schedules may slip or be delayed but the LCP is the more accurate
representation of the load that will be consumed by a large load over the long term, which is the
horizon of both transmission planning and resource adequacy assessment.

                              III.    COMMENTS ON PROPOSED RULE

        A. Proposed Section 25.192(k)(1) – Offset of Interconnection Fees in Revenue
           Requirement

        The proposed Section 25.192(k)(1) would require TSPs to apply “all interconnection fee
amounts” received under the proposed rule relating to large load customer interconnection
standards (i.e., 16 TAC § 25.194), which is pending in another project (Project No. 58481), 19 “as
an offset to the TSP’s transmission revenue requirement.” The Proposed Rule appears to assume
that the interconnection fee will not be refundable in any circumstances, but that issue has not yet
been decided by the Commission in Project No. 58481, as that rulemaking is still pending, and
many commenters (including NRG 20) have recommended that the fee should be at least partially
refundable in some circumstances. Coupled with the proposed minimum billing demand concept
in the instant rulemaking, a non-refundable interconnection fee would be overly punitive and may
chill business development in the state. For the reasons explained above and in the interconnection
standards rulemaking (Project No. 58481), NRG supports policies that strike a balance between
protecting residential customers from the financial burden of large load development while also
incentivizing serious large load customers to come to Texas. In furtherance of those objectives,
NRG continues to support partial refundability of the interconnection fee for large load customers
that actually achieve commercial operation (as it supported in its comments in Project No. 58481)
and, given that the interconnection standards rulemaking is still pending, suggests that the rule
language in proposed Section 25.192(k)(1) be revised to recognize that the fee may end up being
refundable under the version of 16 TAC § 25.194 that is ultimately adopted:

        (k)(1) Interconnection fee. A large load customer must pay the interconnecting
        TSP an interconnection fee in accordance with §25.194 (relating to Large Load
        Interconnection Standards). In all proceedings to adjust rates under this section,
        TSPs must apply all non-refunded interconnection fee amounts received as an offset
        to the TSP's transmission revenue requirement.

       NRG Response: NRG does not recommend this approach. Transmission projects

          NRG ENERGY, INC.'S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY - PROJECT NO. 58000


•   The Legislative goal of including transmission cost allocation in Senate Bill 6 (SB6) was to
    ensure that the average Texan (i.e., the residential customer class) does not bear more than their
    fair share of the costs of transmission investment-i.e., that all loads are "appropriately
    assigned ' and "appropriately contribute" to the recovery ofthose costs .
•   The results from Staff's analysis and NRG's prior comments in Project No. 58484 highlight
    the urgent and immediate need to modify the current 4CP transmission cost allocation
    methodology and move to a methodology that more equitably allocates transmission costs
    among the consumer classes.
•   NRG supports the proposed move from 4CP to 12CP and the change of the duration from 15
    minutes to 30 minutes, but would also support more CPs (such as 52 or 365) and a longer
    duration (such as two hours). NRG also supports the Proposed Rule's evaluation of the CPs on
    a monthly basis (rather than the highest 12 CPs during the year, regardless of when those fall).
•   NRG conceptually supports a minimum billing demand concept for large loads, which could
    be further limited to a larger size threshold for the load that would generally correspond with
    large computational loads (such as 250 MW and up).However, to strike a balance between
    ensuring that large loads appropriately contribute to system upgrade costs without discouraging
    their investment in Texas, and to appropriately recognize the value of, and incentivize, co-
    location (e.g., bring your own generation or BYOG) and other grid friendly arrangements,
    NRG recommends a phased reduction ofthe minimum billing demand across the proposed 20-
    year period for both stand-alone large loads and co-located large loads, with a different starting
    point and reduction schedule for each scenario.
•   Specifically, for large loads that co-locate with existing or new generation or interconnect as a
    provisional controllable load resource (with an associated withdrawal limitation), the
    minimum billing demand should start at 50 percent of contracted demand and then phase down
    in five year increments to 25 percent (years 6 through 10), 15 percent (years 11 through 15),
    and 10 percent (years 16 through 20), with an additional cap on the minimum billing demand
    to reflect any withdrawal limitation imposed as the result of an ERCOT batch process.
    o Notably, to determine any needed transmission system upgrades for a Withdrawal Limited
         Private Use Network (WLPUN), ERCOT will model the arrangement with the generation
        and load together (i.e., with the generation serving the co-located load). Thus, it especially
